questions.enonce_markdown:
Consider the following elements of Group VII (Group 17) of the periodic table: F, Cl, Br, I.

(i) Sketch a graph of bond energy against atomic number for the elements.

Explain the shape of the graph.

(ii) Write balanced chemical equations for the laboratory preparation of HCl and HBr.

HCl:

HBr:

Explain the reason for the similarity or difference in the method of preparation *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Graph.** The bond energy is taken as the energy needed to break the X-X bond of the diatomic molecules $\mathrm{X_2}$ (typical data-book values, not given in the paper):

| Element | F | Cl | Br | I |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Atomic number | 9 | 17 | 35 | 53 |
| X-X bond energy / kJ mol$^{-1}$ | 158 | 242 | 193 | 151 |

Sketch: atomic number on the x-axis (9, 17, 35, 53) and bond energy on the y-axis. The graph **rises from fluorine to a maximum at chlorine, then falls steadily through bromine to iodine**.

*Explanation.*

- **From Cl to I the bond energy decreases.** Going down the group the atoms get larger, so the X-X bond is **longer** and the shared pair is held further from the two nuclei; the overlap of the larger, more diffuse outer orbitals is less effective, and the bond is weaker (Cl$_2$ > Br$_2$ > I$_2$).
- **Fluorine is out of the trend (lower than chlorine).** The F atom is very small, so the F-F bond is very short and the **lone pairs on the two fluorine atoms are very close and repel each other strongly**, which weakens the bond. Chlorine, being larger, has much less lone-pair repulsion, so Cl-Cl is the strongest of the four.

(If the graph is read as the H-X bond energy of the hydrogen halides, it falls steadily from HF to HI for the same reason of increasing bond length.)

**(ii) Laboratory preparation.**

*HCl:* sodium chloride is warmed with concentrated sulphuric acid:

$$\mathrm{NaCl(s)} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaHSO_4(s)} + \mathrm{HCl(g)}$$

*HBr:* sodium (or potassium) bromide is warmed with concentrated **phosphoric(V) acid**, not sulphuric acid:

$$\mathrm{NaBr(s)} + \mathrm{H_3PO_4(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaH_2PO_4(s)} + \mathrm{HBr(g)}$$

*Similarity:* in both cases the hydrogen halide is made by **displacement of a volatile acid from its sodium salt by a concentrated, non-volatile acid** (the gas escapes from the mixture and drives the reaction on).

*Difference and reason:* concentrated sulphuric acid is also an **oxidising agent**. Chloride ion is a very weak reducing agent and is not oxidised, so $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ can be used for HCl. Bromide ion (and the HBr formed) is a **stronger reducing agent** (larger ion, electron lost more easily) and is oxidised by concentrated $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$:

$$2\mathrm{HBr} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \rightarrow \mathrm{Br_2} + \mathrm{SO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}$$

which gives brown bromine vapour and sulphur dioxide and contaminates the product (the yield of HBr is poor). A **non-oxidising acid, concentrated $\mathrm{H_3PO_4}$**, is therefore used for HBr.

questions.enonce_markdown:
In the manufacture of sulphuric acid, $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$, the sulphur trioxide, $\mathrm{SO_3}$, formed is dissolved in already existing concentrated sulphuric acid.

(i) Write an equation for the reaction at this stage.

(ii) Give reasons why water is not added to the sulphur trioxide to produce sulphuric acid *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Sulphur trioxide dissolves in concentrated sulphuric acid to give **oleum** (fuming sulphuric acid, disulphuric acid):

$$\mathrm{SO_3(g)} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_2S_2O_7(l)}$$

(The oleum is then diluted carefully with water to give concentrated sulphuric acid: $\mathrm{H_2S_2O_7} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$.)

**(ii) Why not add water directly?** The reaction $\mathrm{SO_3} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ is **violently exothermic**. The heat released vaporises the water and the acid, producing a **fine, corrosive mist (fog) of sulphuric acid** that does not condense easily, is difficult to collect and handle, escapes in the exit gases and causes pollution and loss of product. Absorbing the $\mathrm{SO_3}$ in concentrated acid is controllable and avoids the mist.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Give the formula of one nitrogenous fertilizer.

(ii) What is the danger of applying more fertilizer to the soil than necessary? *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Ammonium nitrate, $\mathrm{NH_4NO_3}$ (other acceptable answers: ammonium sulphate $(\mathrm{NH_4})_2\mathrm{SO_4}$, urea $\mathrm{CO(NH_2)_2}$).

**(ii) Danger of excess fertilizer.** Nitrate and ammonium ions that the plants cannot take up are very soluble and are **washed (leached) by rain into streams, rivers, lakes and groundwater**. This causes **eutrophication**: the extra nutrients make algae grow explosively (algal bloom); when the algae die, bacteria decompose them and use up the dissolved oxygen, so fish and other aquatic organisms die. Nitrates in drinking water are also harmful (they can cause "blue baby" syndrome), and too much fertilizer may acidify the soil or damage the crops.

The elements of group I and II of the periodic table are called s - block elements.

(i) Write down the outermost electronic configuration of the elements of group I.

(ii) State and explain the trend down the group for the reactions of the Group II (Group 2) elements with water.

Trend:

Explanation:

(iii) Write balanced chemical equations to show the reactions of the following elements with water.

A. Sodium:

B. Magnesium:

(iv) Arrange the hydroxides of Group II elements (Group 2) in increasing order of solubility beginning with the least soluble. *[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The outermost electronic configuration of the Group I elements is $\mathbf{ns^1}$ (one electron in the outer s subshell; for example $3s^1$ for sodium, $4s^1$ for potassium).

**(ii) Trend.** The **reactivity of the Group II elements with water increases down the group**: beryllium does not react even with steam, magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water but burns in steam, calcium reacts steadily with cold water, and strontium and barium react rapidly (vigorously), giving hydrogen and the hydroxide each time.

*Explanation.* Down the group the **atomic radius increases** and the outer electrons are **more shielded** from the nuclear charge by additional inner shells, so the two outer s electrons are held less strongly. The **first and second ionisation energies decrease**, so the atoms lose their electrons (are oxidised to $\mathrm{M^{2+}}$) more easily: the elements become more electropositive and stronger reducing agents, hence more reactive.

**(iii) Equations.**

A. Sodium: $2\mathrm{Na(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}$

B. Magnesium: $\mathrm{Mg(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mg(OH)_2(s)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}$ (very slow with cold water; with steam, $\mathrm{Mg(s)} + \mathrm{H_2O(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgO(s)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}$).

**(iv) Solubility of the Group II hydroxides** increases down the group. In increasing order, starting with the least soluble:

$$\mathrm{Be(OH)_2} < \mathrm{Mg(OH)_2} < \mathrm{Ca(OH)_2} < \mathrm{Sr(OH)_2} < \mathrm{Ba(OH)_2}$$
